(a) Summary of the Paper:
The paper addresses the concern of model theft on untrusted edge devices, which is a key barrier to the wider adoption of LLMs. Unlike existing TEE-based secure inference methods that generally suffer from statistical vulnerabilities, the authors propose LoRO, a method designed to protect on-device LLMs. LoRO incorporates two main components:
  (i) Low-Rank Masking – completely obfuscates model parameters while enabling faster inference through low-rank computation in TEE. The approach introduces no accuracy loss and requires neither retraining nor model modification.
  (ii) Factor Multiplexing – mitigates additional latency caused by secure memory paging by reducing the secure memory footprint.
With these techniques, LoRO effectively downgrades on-device LLMs to black-box level (achieving 0.94× MS accuracy) while still delivering real-time inference performance (1.49× latency, compared to 112× in existing SOTA methods).

(b) Strengths:
The reviewers highlighted several strengths of the paper:
   -Novelty of the proposed approach (Reviewer PcW2).
   -Logical flow and clarity of the presentation (Reviewer eg2Y).
   -Strong theoretical analysis and comprehensive literature summary (Reviewer Wwxk).
  -Clear and logical organization of the paper (Reviewer tpNN).

(c) Weaknesses:
The main concerns raised by reviewers include:
-Limited experiments on challenging datasets.
-The need for additional technical clarity in some parts.
-Require additional experiments under critical or adversarial settings.
- One of the reviewer also raised a few issues related to the writing. 

(d) Justification for Decision:
Three reviewers recommended acceptance and one suggested borderline accept. The paper address a timely problem of secure and efficient on-device LLM inference.  The proposed method demonstrates both novelty and practicality, with theoretical and empirical evidence. Overall, the strengths of the  paper clearly outweigh the weaknesses, and I recommend acceptance.

(e) Rebuttal and Discussion Summary:
During the rebuttal, the authors addressed the concerns raised by the reviewers with additional analysis and experiments. All four reviewers agreed that their concerns had been adequately addressed and indicated a preference for acceptance. The Area Chair concurs with the reviewers’ assessment.

The authors are expected to incorporate all additional experiments and clarifications provided during the rebuttal into the revised manuscript, as promised. They should also fix the minor writing issues noted by reviewers and open-source the code as stated in the manuscript.

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely appreciate your recognition of our work and your positive remarks regarding our writing organization. Your insightful feedback is highly valuable to us. We now address your concerns point-by-point below:

>**Q1:** The effectiveness of MSP attacks largely hinges on the statistical similarity between publicly available pretrained models and the target private model. However, the degree of this similarity—and its consistency across different model architectures, tasks, and fine-tuning strategies—can vary significantly. A more in-depth discussion on the origins and extent of this similarity would strengthen the paper.

**R1:** We deeply appreciate this valuable perspective. While the concept of leveraging statistical similarity for attacks **was initially proposed in TEESlice [12]**, that work focused exclusively on small CV models and **did not extend attacks to LLMs**. Modern LLMs architectures (typically Transformer variants) exhibit well-documented high similarity in both parameter and representation spaces [7, Ref 1]. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in proprietary domain fine-tuned models [Ref 2]. **Based on these observations, this work represents the first successful extension of such attacks to LLMs, revealing critical security vulnerabilities in existing TEE-based secure inference.**

Notably，our MSP attack only requires parameter distribution to estimate TEE-shielded model secrets. To address your concern directly, we intentionally attacked RoBERTa using BERT as the pretrained model (RoBERTa's training data significantly exceeds BERT's, with typical parameter similarity around 40%). As shown in the table below, SOTA TLG remains vulnerable to MSP attacks, while our proposed LoRO achieves performance comparable to black-box settings:

| Model   | Dataset | TLG    | LoRO   | Black-Box |
|:-------:|:-------:|:------:|:------:|:---------:|

We sincerely thank you for your insightful feedback and constructive critiques. Your appreciation for our theoretical analysis is deeply encouraging. Below are our point-by-point responses to your concerns (some weaknesses are addressed alongside related questions):

> **W1:** The MSP attack requires extensive prior knowledge. While this assumption is reasonable for LLMs—since most are open-source and fine-tuned from publicly available models—it may not hold for small models and ViTs. These models often lack such vulnerabilities, making the success of the MSP attack on them questionable.

**R1:** Thank you for this valuable observation. We have now supplemented our evaluation with **Model Stealing with Prior (MSP) experiments on ViT and ResNet18 (small model)**. For model prior knowledge, we used model trained on CIFAR10. Due to time constraints during rebuttal response, we did not find a perfect way to adapt TLG to CNNs.

| Model| Dataset  | TLG    | SOTER  | Magnitude | ShadowNet | Black-Box |
|-|----------|--------|--------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| ViT-Base | CIFAR100 | 89.67% | 88.30% | 87.28%    | 79.27%    | 14.57%    |
| ViT-Base | Food101  | 81.51% | 75.52% | 80.05%    | 71.90%    | 10.28%    |
| ResNet18 | CIFAR100 | N/A    | 67.30% | 73.55%    | 65.42%    | 14.74%    |

As shown in the table above, **MSP remains effective for small models like ViT and ResNet18**. This is not surprising, since prior work [7,12] have attacked small models successfully. Our contribution lies in **extending this attack to more challenging LLMs via rigorous statistical analysis**.

> **W2:** The proposed LoRO appears to be a combination of several existing techniques: the low-rank mask resembles the use of Freivalds’ algorithm in Slalom [a], the permutation matrix is directly adopted from TransLinkGuard [13], and the factor multiplexing is similar to the cornerstone fingerprints in SOTER [9].

**R2:** We appreciate your careful analysis. While surface similarities exist, LoRO’s core mechanisms differ fundamentally:  

1. **Freivalds vs. Our Low-Rank Mask**. As shown in the Table below, the objective and mechnism of two methdos are different. Actually, we are inspired of Parameter-Efficient-Fine-Tune(PEFT) [b] to develop the idea of low-rank mask.
   
| Technique | Objective| Mechnism |
|-|-|-|
| Freivalds' algorithm | Verify the integrity of outsourced computation |$P (A\times B \times r=C\times r \| A\times B \neq C) < \epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is very small. Hence verify the result $C=A\times B ?$ efficiently. |
| Low-Rank Mask| Obfuscate LLM parameters | $W'=W+BA$ to obfuscate $W$|

2. **TLG Permutation vs. Our Permutation**. TransLinkGuard [13] uses permutation to obfuscate parameters as $W'=\pi^T W$. As analyzed in Section 4.1, it is vulnerable to intermediate-result analysis, which can cause leakage of $\pi$ and then de-obfuscate $W'$. In contrast, our permutation **only protects Attention Block intermediate results as $Q=\pi^T Q$** (similar to OTP but adapted for transformers). Crucially, **LoRo secures parameters via Low-Rank Mask as $W'=W+BA$, preventing recovery even if $\pi$ are compromised.**

3. **SOTER Fingerprints vs. Factor Multiplexing**. While both use linear combinations, their purposes and mechnism diverge:  
   - SOTER/TSQP [7,9]: Generate challenge-response pairs for *computation integrity*, based on the associativity.
   - Our approach: Minimize secure memory overhead for **Low-Rank Mask storage**, and is not related to associativity.

**In conclusion, the shared mathematical concept serves for distinct security objectives, and is different in mechnism.**

> **W3 & Q4:** (W3) LoRO lacks result verification for outsourced computation, a feature provided by methods like TEESlice [12, 31] and SOTER [9]. (Q4) How does LoRO ensure the correctness of outsourced computation?

**R3:** Thank you for highlighting this. While LoRO focuses on TEE-based obfuscation, it **fully supports two established integrity methods: Challenge-Response**[7,9] and **Freivalds' algorithm[a,12,31]**:  

To solve your concern, **we evaluate the Challenge-Response Method [7,9] on LoRO**. Experimental results show that LoRO achieves **100% fault injection detection accuracy under INT-8, with no false positive.** Under FLOAT-32, we observe only one false positive, which can be resolvable via error-threshold tuning.


> **W4 & Q1 & Q2:**  (W4) Some attack details are missing. In Section 4, the paper outlines the attack pipeline for three types of obfuscation methods but lacks specific details on how ShadowNet’s obfuscation is broken—particularly since it employs both multiplicative and additive masking on weights. The explanation in Appendix A is also unclear. Additionally, it is not sufficiently explained how the proposed LoRO is attacked. Since the attacker cannot recover the exact weights, is the attack conducted using techniques from TransLinkGuard [13]? (Q1) How is the MSP attack implemented for LoRO? (Q2) How is ShadowNet’s obfuscation broken?

**R4:** We appreciate this request for clarification and will introduce them as follows: 

1. **Attack on ShadowNet.** ShadowNet’s obfuscation: $W'=W\times \lambda+F$. Since $F$ is dense ($F$ of Magnitude is sparse), the introduced computation in TEE is costly, so it’s offloaded to REE. Following the TEESlice [12, 31], we first remove the mask $F$, and then estimate $\lambda$ via variance analysis (Appendix A). Finally,  we fine-tune the model with a small dataset.

2. **Attack on LoRO.** Since LoRO exhibit no real parameters, we evaluate three attack strategies:  
   - (1) **LoRA-like fine-tune**: Initialize parameters using obfuscated weights, and optimize $BA$ through small datasets to achieve model stealing [b].
   - (2) **REE-parameter initialization**: We directly use REE parameters to initialize model and conduct fully finetune.
   - (3) **Black-box**: Standard black-box Knockoff attack with random initialization.
  
   Experimental results show that **(1) outperforms (2)**, so we report the result of (1) and (3) in Table 1.

>**W5:** Some evaluations are missing. In Section 6.3, the paper compares efficiency with a few full shielding methods and SOTER. While comparing with full shielding approaches is reasonable, since they offer similar black-box security and the performance gains of LoRO are somewhat expected. The evaluation only includes SOTER, overlooking other methods listed in Table 1. Additionally, it does not compare with TEESlice, which is also applicable to LLMs [31].

**R5:** Thank you for this suggestion. We now provide comprehensive efficiency comparisons and discuss TEESlice:  

**Efficiency Comparison.** Due to code availability, initial submission only compared with SOTER. We have now implemented other baselines on SGX. As shown in the Table below, LoRO’s latency is comparable to TLG, while TLG cannot provide black-box security. Since OTP is not applicable, we remove it from attention block protection in magnitude and shadownet. We also notice that other methods suffer critical slowdowns since:  
  - MLCapsule: Secure paging overhead  
  - SOTER: Activation computation 
  - Magnitude: Sparse computation in TEE is too heavyweight for large scale LLMs

|Model|MLCapsule|SOTER|ShadowNet|Magnitude|TLG|LoRO
|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
|RoBERTa-B|54.08x|1.34x|2.35x|8.92x|1.10x|1.12x|
|BART-L|95.17x|1.62x|2.48x|10.33x|1.14x|1.18x|
|Qwen2-7B|321.58x|2.01x|3.60x|35.84x|1.59x|1.64x|
| LaMA3.2-8B|358.60x|2.10x|3.75x|37.67x|1.70x|1.77x|


**Discussion on TEESlice.** While TEESlice [12] pioneered model stealing defenses on small models, its journal version [31] requires **replacing transformer attention with linear attention** for OTP compatibility. This introduces accuracy drops and expensive retraining costs, making it **incompatible with mainstream LLMs (e.g., LLaMA, Qwen)**. So it's **difficult for us to compare with TEESlice on mainstream LLMs**. In contrast, LoRO preserves model architecture and offers broader applicability.

>**W6:** Typos and writting mistakes.

**R6**. We sincerely appreciate your meticulous proofreading. We have corrected:  
1. Eq. 3 revised to $y = x'W' - xD - o(W + D)$ (with $x'$ defined in text)  
2. Eq. 4 revised to $y = x'W' - xBA - o(W + BA)$  
3. Added citations in Table 1: TLG [13], ShadowNet [10], Magnitude [8], SOTER [9]  
4. Revised Table 1 highlights  
5. Fixed references to Table 1/Appendix C  

We are conducting additional rounds of proofreading to eliminate residual errors.

> **Q3** Since LoRO uses the same additive masking technique described in Section 4.2, does it suffer from the same vulnerabilities?

**R7**: Thank you for this important question. We will analyze the security in detail:

The additive mask: $W'=W+D$ itself is considered secure，as the OTP introduced by Slalom [a] is stil secure nowadays. But de-obfuscate the results in TEE requires to compute $xD$, which is equivalent to full inference in TEE. To avoid the high latency, existing methods introduce:

- Magnitude: sparsifies $D$, which introduces gradient anomaly.
- ShadowNet: offload $D$ to REE for acceleration.

Proposed LoRO dose not expose $D$ to REE, and apply dense mask on all parameters. Hence, LoRO dose not suffer from the same vulnerabilities.

> We are profoundly grateful for your time and expertise. Your feedback has significantly strengthened our work. All revisions above will be incorporated into the manuscript. Should any concerns remain, we would be honored to address them.

Reference

[a] Tramer, Florian, and Dan Boneh. "Slalom: Fast, verifiable and private execution of neural networks in trusted hardware." arXiv preprint arXiv:1806.03287 (2018).

[b] Hu E J, Shen Y, Wallis P, et al. Lora: Low-rank adaptation of large language models[J]. ICLR, 2022, 1(2): 3.

summary.value: This paper focuses on the problem of model stealing attacks that can occur when running LLMs on untrusted devices such as edge devices. This paper first proposes an MSP attack, indicating that the existing protection method using TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) suffers from statistical vulnerabilities and may be exploited by the attacker. Therefore, this paper proposes a new method LoRO, which completely fuzzes the model parameters through the dense masking mechanism, including using low rank factors to generate dense masks, improving inference efficiency, and sharing low rank factors across multiple layers to reduce memory consumption.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

- Trendy topic
- Well-organized paper
- Easy to follow

Weaknesses:

- More clarifications are needed

questions.value:
This paper is well-organized, and the writing and charts are very clear and easy to understand, and the Threat Model is also described clearly. LoRO is simple but effective, with low performance loss, and does not require model structure modification or retraining. Although this method increases the memory requirements of the device, this paper also proposes Factor Multiplexing to reduce the memory. But I still have some concerns:

1. In the pipeline of MSP attack, the attacker used a small dataset for fine-tuning. Whether this part of the small dataset is a subset of figure1 (a) Private Dataset or a dataset that is completely another domain.
2. In Figure 2, it is unclear what each point in the t-SNE visualization represents. Are they column vectors from the weight matrices of each model layer? I believe the authors should clarify this explicitly in the figure caption.
3. Consider that Factor Multiplexing reduces storage pressure, it will introduce new computational or runtime costs. The paper should provide a more detailed analysis of this trade-off.
4. In Table 3, LoRO shows almost no performance drop across several datasets, such as SQuAD and GSM8K. However, I wonder how well it would perform on more challenging benchmarks, for example, the MATH dataset [1].
5. Since LoRO places key components inside the TEE, side-channel attacks are a very realistic threat in deployment. Any such leakage could directly expose the shared low-rank basis factors used for parameter obfuscation.

Overall, I think this motivation is sufficient and the proposed method is also very effective.

Minors:

1. It should be clearly written in Table1's caption that this is the result of evaluation under the MSP attack.

Reference:

1. Dan Hendrycks et al. “Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset.” NeurIPS 2021.

summary.value: This paper presents a secure inference framework for LLMs using TEE. It employs additive masking and a one-time pad for matrix obfuscation, incorporates a permutation matrix to protect scaled dot-product operations, and applies factor multiplexing to optimize memory usage. Experimental results show strong resistance to model-stealing attacks and reduced latency compared to existing approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- Analyzes the risks of current methods and proposes a new attack to demonstrate them.
- Evaluation and visualization effectively demonstrate both security and efficiency.
- Provides a thorough analysis and comprehensive summary of existing work.

Weaknesses:
- The MSP attack requires extensive prior knowledge. While this assumption is reasonable for LLMs—since most are open-source and fine-tuned from publicly available models—it may not hold for small models and ViTs. These models often lack such vulnerabilities, making the success of the MSP attack on them questionable.

- The proposed LoRO appears to be a combination of several existing techniques: the low-rank mask resembles the use of Freivalds’ algorithm in Slalom [a], the permutation matrix is directly adopted from TransLinkGuard [13], and the factor multiplexing is similar to the cornerstone fingerprints in SOTER [9].

- LoRO lacks result verification for outsourced computation, a feature provided by methods like TEESlice [12, 31] and SOTER [9].

- Some attack details are missing. In Section 4, the paper outlines the attack pipeline for three types of obfuscation methods but lacks specific details on how ShadowNet’s obfuscation is broken—particularly since it employs both multiplicative and additive masking on weights. The explanation in Appendix A is also unclear. Additionally, it is not sufficiently explained how the proposed LoRO is attacked. Since the attacker cannot recover the exact weights, is the attack conducted using techniques from TransLinkGuard [13]? 
- Some evaluations are missing. In Section 6.3, the paper compares efficiency with a few full shielding methods and SOTER. While comparing with full shielding approaches is reasonable, since they offer similar black-box security and the performance gains of LoRO are somewhat expected. The evaluation only includes SOTER, overlooking other methods listed in Table 1. Additionally, it does not compare with TEESlice, which is also applicable to LLMs [31].

[a] Tramer, Florian, and Dan Boneh. "Slalom: Fast, verifiable and private execution of neural networks in trusted hardware." arXiv preprint arXiv:1806.03287 (2018).

Some Mistakes and Suggestions:
- In Equations 3 and 4, the variable should be x instead of x', as x' is not introduced until line 223.
- Missing citations. In Tables 1 and 2, it would be better to include citations for the baseline methods directly in the tables to improve readability, especially for newcomers to the field. Some abbreviations, such as TLG for TransLinkGuard, differ from the original paper titles. While defining such abbreviations is acceptable, proper citations are still necessary.
- Incorrect highlighting. In Table 1, it states “the worst is in red,” but several red-highlighted values are not the highest. For example, in the RoBERTa model on the SST-2 dataset, SOTER’s 93.20% is higher than the red-highlighted 91.42%. Similarly, for the BART model: on the MRPC dataset, SOTER’s 82.11% is higher than the red 79.96%; on the SST-2 dataset, SOTER’s 94.57% is higher than the red 91.05%.
- Incorrect table references. In lines 44, 186, 279, and 500, “Table 1” is incorrectly linked to Section 1 instead of jumping to the actual table. Additionally, in lines 282 and 519, “Table C” is mentioned, which appears to be a mistake—it likely refers to “Table 6”, but is incorrectly linked to Table 5.

questions.value:
1. How is the MSP attack implemented for LoRO?
2. How is ShadowNet’s obfuscation broken?
3. Since LoRO uses the same additive masking technique described in Section 4.2, does it suffer from the same vulnerabilities?
4. How does LoRO ensure the correctness of outsourced computation?

final_justification.value:
The author rebuttal fully addressed my concerns:

1. Regarding novelty, the authors clearly articulate the differences between the proposed LoRO and previous works, demonstrating its novelty and effectiveness.
2. For baselines, the authors provide additional experiments showing its superior efficiency compared to prior methods.
3. On verification for outsourced computation, the authors conducted further evaluations.

With all concerns addressed, I raise my score to Accept.

summary.value: This paper focuses on the risk of model theft faced by large language models when deployed on untrustworthy edge devices. To address this growing problem, the authors propose a novel secure reasoning framework, LoRO, which is built on top of the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) and aims to provide a language model reasoning solution for edge devices that combines real-time, high-precision, and strong protection of model intellectual property.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
- The problem addressed in the paper - deploying LLM safely and efficiently on edge devices - is one of the core challenges facing the AI field today. It has important practical significance and application prospects.
- The author demonstrates excellent logical organization and clarity of expression in writing the paper. The article is well structured and able to lead the reader to a smooth understanding of the research motivation and technical realization of the paper.

Weaknesses
- The effectiveness of MSP attacks largely hinges on the statistical similarity between publicly available pretrained models and the target private model. However, the degree of this similarity—and its consistency across different model architectures, tasks, and fine-tuning strategies—can vary significantly. A more in-depth discussion on the origins and extent of this similarity would strengthen the paper.
- While the low-rank design offers clear benefits in terms of efficiency, it also raises a critical concern: could this architectural choice inadvertently open up vulnerabilities that are specific to low-rank structures?
- In the evaluation setup of MSP attacks, the small dataset available to the attacker—reportedly around 10% of the original training set—serves as a critical factor influencing the attack's effectiveness. However, the paper lacks a sensitivity analysis on how the performance of the attack varies with respect to the size, quality, and relevance of this dataset to the target model’s data.

title.value: LoRO: Real-Time on-Device Secure Inference for LLMs via TEE-Based Low Rank Obfuscation

TLDR.value: We analyze and compromise existing TEE-based secure inference methods by our Model Stealing attacks with Prior, and propose a novel secure inference method named LoRO, which is efficient, secure and accurate.

abstract.value: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained remarkable success, they are consistently at risk of being stolen when deployed on untrusted edge devices. As a solution, TEE-based secure inference has been proposed to protect valuable model property. However, we identify a statistical vulnerability in existing protection methods, and furtherly compromise their security guarantees by proposed Model Stealing Attack with Prior. To eliminate this vulnerability, LoRO is presented in this paper, which leverages dense mask to completely obfuscate parameters. LoRO includes two innovations: (1) Low Rank Mask, which uses low-rank factors to generate dense masks efficiently. The computing complexity in TEE is hence reduced by an exponential amount to achieve inference speed up, while providing robust model confidentiality. (2) Factors Multiplexing, which reuses several cornerstone factors to generate masks for all layers. Compared to one-mask-per-layer, the secure memory requirement is reduced from GB-level to tens of MB, hence avoiding the hundred-fold latency introduced by secure memory paging. Experimental results indicate that LoRO achieve a $0.94\times$ Model Stealing (MS) accuracy, while SOTA methods presents $3.37\times$ at least. The averaged inference latency of LoRO is only $1.49\times$, compared to the $112\times$ of TEE-shielded inference. Moreover, LoRO results no accuracy loss, and requires no re-training and structure modification. LoRO can solve the concerns regarding model thefts on edge devices in an efficient and secure manner, facilitating the wide edge application of LLMs.
